speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege with reference to an article published in the " Evenement," on April 12, last.
With large headlines this newspaper publishes what follows: Mr. J. F. Pouliot interrupted by cries of "Taschereau, Taschereau" and " who placed the bomb."
The question of privilege refers to the following extract:
An incident
An ever youthful member from ou.r province distinguishes himself at Ottawa by wild sallies against the Prime Minister of Quebec. Last night, the House of Commons clearly manifested that he would be the gainer by becoming somewhat more discreet. His speech interrupted by a devil of a noise, became almost as unintelligible as unintelligent. The opposition having taken up the cry of Taschereau, the Govern-

C.N.R.-Railway and Shipping Committee
ment side replied by applauses. While our fiery member once more sat down, happy of having created a storm. But it was a storm of laughter.
The " Evenement " passes for a business newspaper.
Has it not an upward scale of rates for lostly publicity?
Is it true that the first come, in that newspaper, may be bombarded. Your Honour, for one dollar; Your Lordship, for two dollars; Your Excellency, for three dollars; Your Highness, for four dollars, and Your Imperial Highness, for five dollars.
The downward scale for cheap and popular publicity is in that newspaper very amusing.
Is it true that one may be called a Governor for half a dollar; Colonel for a quarter; that for ten cents they shine your boots, and for five cents they lick them?
From July 1, last, the Quebec government has paid for printing and publicity $9,961.38 to this newspaper, whose president, Mr. J. H. For.tier, the directing soul of the P. T. Legare establishment, loudly clamours for protection so as to sell agricultural implements dearer to farmers.
If this is a business paper it is a slot machine paper.
A what?

A slot machine paper. It insinuates that on Thursday last I attacked the Premier of Quebec in the house. In fact I did not. When I asked-referring to Sir Robert Borden-"Who was the greatest man in the Tory party?"-the gentlemen on your left, Mr. .Speaker, answered, "Taschereau, Taschereau". I said nothing unpleasant in reference to him that evening because one of his children was married in .the morning of the same day, and it is on account of that social function that I observed that truce which L'Evenement has not seen fit to respect.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext:
Before the motion is put, I wish
to observe that, looking through the proceedings in past years, it occurs to me that as this house" represents the shareholders of the Canadian National system and sets up this committee as a committee of those shareholders to deal with the accounts and the transaction of the business of the system, no limitation should be placed upon the right of the committee to deal with the whole of what I might call the operations of the system during the year, which would arise out of the discussion of the accounts, if construed an a large way, with respect to employment and many other matters which it is uneoessary for me at the moment to mention, but which any shareholder would have the right to discuss in the case of a private company. I take it that this committee should have all the powers which the shareholders of a private company would have in discussing the business of such an enterprise in which they were interested; for the real weakness of our system of government ownership lies in the difficulty of the shareholders in making themselves articulate so far as the transaction of their business is concerned. In other words, this parliament is the nearest approach we have to the shareholders in a private enterprise, and this committee should be regarded as a committee of shareholders to discuss the accounts, the estimates and the transaction of the business of the enterprise during the twelve months for which those accounts are placed before the committee.

I think the description
which my hon. friend has just given of what the activities of the committee should be is a correct description of what the activities of the committee have been in fact in the past______
With some limitation.

-with one qualification which arises from the peculiar condition to which my hon. friend has just referred. The shareholders of a private company would of course be free at all times to discuss any matter affecting the business of the company, but they would also be free to determine that it
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

was not wise for publicity to be given to any particular item of that discussion. More or less frequently in connection with the proceedings of the special committee during my experience of it-and I presume prior to that time also-there have arisen for discussion matters respecting which the management desired that the committee should have full information but which the management did not desire to become public property In all such cases the committee has, I think, agreed to have the information given to the committee itself but not made a matter of record. That has very frequently happened. Perhaps I am exaggerating when I say very frequently," but at any rate it hits happened on numerous occasions, and I do not think there will be any disposition on the part of the management to adopt any other attitude in the future. It is of course a little embarrassing, as my hon. friend will see, because of the broad right of inquiry which parliament undoubtedly has. Parliament could publish from the housetops any and every detail of the Canadian National's business if it so desired; but this is not considered desirable for the same reason that it is not considered desirable in connection with some aspects and details of an ordinary private corporation's business.

While it is improper
under the rules for me to make further observations, I desire to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that I entirely agree with what the minister has said. So far as the shareholders of a private company are concerned they do not keep records of their speeches to be transmitted to the public; it is merely a shareholders' record. As regards the record, therefore, I am not so much concerned about that as about the powers of the committee to represent the shareholders in their entirety in dealing with the business of the system.

Undoubtedly.
Motion agreed to;

Mr. J. A. CLARK (Vancouver-Burrard) moved the second reading of Bill No. 85, for the relief of Effie Margaret Hill.

On several occasions last year I objected to divorce bills being

Procedure respecting Divorce
passed in this manner. I know nothing whatever with regard to the bill now before the house-and that indeed is one reason why I think I should oppose its passing the house. The member who moved this bill may have some information with regard to it, and if so I think he should give it in detail to this house. Later on I shall insist upon such a statement being made and until that information is forthcoming and the house is fully apprised of the details, I do not think we should be asked to pass the bill.

The hon. member must
have the evidence.

I have in my desk the evidence relating to some sixty divorce cases, and I venture to say that no member of the house has read every bit of that evidence. If he has, I would suggest that he is very much in the position of a garbage can and would hardly be fit to participate in the discussions of the house. I frankly confess that I have not read the particulars relating to any one of these bills, and I know nothing whatever about the particular bill now before the house. I venture to say that nine-tenths of the members are in precisely the same position.
Ninetynine hundredths.

And yet we are
asked to vote in favour of the bill. I am rather sorry for the parties concerned in this bill, because it may be inferred by the general public that there is some outstanding reason for the challenging of this particular case. I assure them that I select this bill simply because it is the first one on the order paper. I desire to test the house on a question of principle rather than on the merits of this particular case.
A few weeks ago the house rejected a bill which provided for a divorce court for the province of Ontario. Under the rules of the house I am precluded from discussing that bill, but I would point out that the rejection by the house of that bill puts us in a different position from that in which we were last year. In the debate on the Senate bill the majority of the members of the house took a very high moral stand with regard to divorce when they rejected that bill on the ground that it was improper that any divorce should be granted. All I can say is that if it is wrong on principle to grant divorces we should reject this 'bill and the many others which follow it. On that occasion members on both sides of the house took the high ground of maintaining the sanctity of the
family. Their argument places some of us in the rather awkward position of seeming to condone the evils of divorce and thus assisting in loosening the family ties. I think I could make out a very good case if I should attempt to prove that those who opposed that bill are the people whose action is tending to loosen the family ties and further increase the evils of divorce.
I am opposed to divorces as granted by this parliament. There has been a greater increase in the number of divorces in the province of Ontario, where there is no divorce court, than in the other provinces of Canada which have such courts. That is one ground for asserting that those who opposed the establishment of a divorce court could easily be accused of increasing the number of divorces. In making that statement I do not consider the number of divorces which have been granted in Detroit and other American cities to residents of the province of Ontario. I will be very frank and say that I am not opposed to divorce under certain circumstances, but I know there are friends of mine here in the house who are opposed to the granting of divorces under any circumstance. We talk about the evils of divorce, but I think we ought rather to talk about the evils of marriage, because, after all, it is the failure of marriage that makes the appeal for divorce necessary. In my view, to force people to live together where there is infidelity, and I would go further and say, where all affection has ceased to exist, is very little less than to force them t-o live in what I might term a state of legalized prostitution. I do not want to be guilty of forcing anyone to continue to live such a life, and hence, under certain circumstances, I am in favour of divorce. It is an intolerable situation that a woman should be compelled to continue to be the wife of a man whom she must despise and where her private life must be simply an inferno on earth. If the opportunity occurred in a properly constituted court, I should be glad to do anything I could to relieve the condition of women or of men so placed.
I should like, as briefly as I can, to enumerate some of my objections to the passing of this bill and of other bills of a similiar character wdiich are before us. In the first place, I object to being a mere rubber stamp, and under the circumstances which now exist, that is the position in which all the members of the House of Commons are placed. Let us examine the procedure for a moment. In Ontario and Quebec and, until further action is taken by Prince Edward Island, also in that province, the only way
Procedure respecting Divorce

in which a divorce can be obtained is by coming to parliament and presenting a bill which must be passed through the regular stages, the three readings in this house and the three readings in the senate. As we all know, these bills in practice go first to the senate and are examined by the Senate committee. I believe this year two senate committees are running concurrently and if space were available, there would be three committees, so great is the pressure of these bills. These are reported by the senate committee to the senate and afterwards in due course they come to the House of Commons. At the present time I am not a member of the private bills committee, but for some years I was, and I know that when these bills came before the private bills committee of this house, they passed in batches just as they are passing their first and second readings in this house. Except on very rare occasions there was no examination whatever of the merits of the bills. In fact often, we even had to gc to considerable trouble to secure a sufficient number of the members of the private bills committee to constitute a quorum in order that in five minutes we might pass twenty, thirty or forty private bills. As every hon. member knows, we have never had a discussion in the house as to the merits of a particular divorce bill; a few days ago there was placed in our mail boxes the evidence in the case of forty-five bills, and this morning I received something like twenty additional bills. This would indicate that sixty-five divorce bills are now before us, and I understand that in the course of the session we shall have over two hnudred more than that. This procedure is becoming a veritable farce. We simply go through the motions and it seems that that is inimical to the best interests of the country as well as demoralizing ho the house itself.
In the second place, the laws of evidence are not very closely adhered to in the senate committee. In so saying, I am not casting any reflection upon the senate committee. I have heard the members of that committee freely discuss the matter. In a properly constituted court the judges have had a good deal of experience in sizing up evidence. On the senate committee there are members who have not been judges, some who have not been lawyers, and who are not accustomed to the careful weighing of evidence. I do not pretend to be a legal expert, but on one occasion when I sat for a short time in that committee, I think the procedure would have been considered in any court to be very lax.
I would hate to be tried for my life or to have my liberty at stake and to be tried under 
the laws of evidence which often prevail in the divorce committee of the senate.
The hon. member would not have a chance.

That may be. I think the hon. member for South Toronto is quite right. I would have no chance at all. Further than that, the evidence so-called is all printed and is circulated among the members of both houses. This involves a very heavy expenditure which would not be involved in the ordinary courts where, as I understand the matter, the evidence is frequently taken down in shorthand but is not extended, unless there is some special reason for doing so. Not only is there a greatly added expense, but the evidence so published consists really of obscene literature. I ventured to say last year and I repeat to-day that those reports could not go through His Majesty's mails if wha.t they contained were known. We could not discuss the details of that evidence on the floor of the house without ordering that the galleries be cleared, and it may be necessary before we are through with this matter to ask that we have a private session in order to discuss some of these cases. That evidence is circulated among the members and is generally thrown into the waste paper baskets. I confess I have some qualms of conscience in doing that because members of the cleaning staff, pages and others, may pick it out of the waste paper baskets and get free obscene literature such as could not be offered for sale in the bookstores in any city of Canada.

The hon. member said he
had not read the evidence.

I have not read it this year. I have looked into it in other years. Last year I read several cases with very great care. I have heard members remarking jocosely that this was very spicy literature. I think, on the other hand, it is revoltingly, disgustingly-
Rotten.

-yes, rotten. That is a very good word which an hon. membef has suggested. The evidence consists of sordid details, stripped of all romance of every kind and presented with a stark reality that is absolutely repellent to any except the most morbid minds.
I abject to the present procedure because poor people cannot come to Ottawa to avail themselves of the divorce court here. It remains a privilege of the better-to-do, unless people happen to be located close to Ottawa.

Supposing somebody resides in Windsor: it means a very heavy expenditure to travel and to bring witnesses all the way from Windsor to Ottawa. It means the employment of a lawyer in Windsor and, under present practice, the employment of a local lawyer in Ottawa. In this way the drain upon the purse of the poor individual seeking divorce is very heavy.
Further, the poor man who is charged with being guilty of a crime that calls for divorce has no opportunity of defending himself. The other day a man wrote me from a town in western Ontario alleging that he had been framed by his wife, who sought a divorce. He said, "I am a poor man. I cannot afford to leave my job and travel to Ottawa. The only evidence against me is that submitted by professional spies, professional detectives," and so on the evidence of two professional detectives the wife was granted a divorce, the husband having no opportunity whatever of appearing in his own behalf. I do not think that is fair. The senate committee may be all right in the case of the wealthy, but it is not fair for the poor people in this country.
I am told that in some of the provinces such as Nova Scotia there is an official connected with the divorce court known as the king's proctor, who represents the public. He is there to draw out any evidence that he sees fit, to see that fair play is being accorded. We have no official of that kind whatever, and it seems to me that here again our procedure facilitates divorce much more than is the case under the ordinary procedure of the courts where certain safeguards are provided. Again, in some of the provincial courts-I do not know whether this is true of all the provinces-there is a period of delay after the case has been tried and before the decree is granted. It is sometimes found that when people have got to the point where a divorce is imminent, the trial brings them to their senses as they realize the alternative, and it is possible to effect a reconciliation. But in the case of divorces by this parliament, once the evidence is heard, the decree immediately goes into force and a divorce from that time is inevitable. I would say that the practice of the provincial courts is highly preferable to the practice we have in this parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend
permit me? I have been away a long time this session, but if I am not wrong this question has been settled by parliament at this very session, and therefore it is hardly in order for my hon. friend to plead for the
Procedure respecting Divorce
establishment of divorce courts when parliament has already declared against them at this very session.

I do not know that I am pleading for the establishment of such a court, but I am pointing out the weaknesses that inhere in our present practice and that pertain to the very case upon which we are asked to decide to-day. I will, however, try to confine myself as closely as possible to the matters that are before the house at this time. I would say that in this case, and in all these cases, we are making no provision whatever for alimony. In the case of the wife being granted the divorce, she goes out without having any claim whatever on the man who was formerly her husband.
How about the man?

The man is in the
same position, but he is supposed to be able to support himself, and perhaps under our existing social conditions he can support himself a little more easily because he has no longer a wife who is dependent upon him.
Sometimes.

I was given an
instance the other day by one of the members of the senate divorce committee. A poor little woman was granted a divorce from her husband. It came out in the evidence, which is locked up in our desks now, I presume, that her husband had communicated to her a venereal disease. The woman is to be granted a divorce under the recommendations of the senate divorce committee, but she goes out without having any redress whatever, without having any provision for ali-monv, and I presume that if she is to secure anything she will have to take a civil action in the regular way in the provincial courts. It is not right that that should be the case, and I intend to do this year as I did last year in regard to some of these cases, and that is to offer amendments making some provision for alimony. I know that hon. members may rise and object that that is ultra vires of the Dominion parliament. Someone asks me why. Because it would trench upon civil rights, but it appears that we ought to do what was done in at least one case in the earlier history of this house and make some provision for alimony.
More serious still, there is no provision whatever in these cases-and wre have forty-five of them before us in this list-for the maintenance of the children.

Is it. beyond our powers to do so?
Procedure respecting Divorce

That is a matter for constitutional lawyers It is a question whether or nut if we pass a measure of this kind it would be an infringment upon civil rights, which under the British North America Act is a matter of provincial concern. That is another of the anomalies under the British North America Act.
Is it beyond the powers of the senate committee?

I understand that in the very early days of divorce legislation by this parliament there was at least one case in which alimony and maintenance for the children was granted, but I think there were only one or possibly two such cases.
But they have the power.

That is not clear. That power has been challenged by constitutional lawyers. I do not know that any test case has been before the courts.
Again, I pointed out in at least one case last year that the man, according to the evidence, was nothing less than a brute, and had committed a crime that made him liable to a penitentiary life sentence. That man was allowed to go free, but as a matter of fact I understand he skipped out to the United States, but he was allowed to go there with, inferentially, the right to marry again and repeat his crime and ruin another life. The senate committee took no action in that respect, and we took no action. There is no provision that action could be taken in those circumstances.
It has been stated by the newspapers that I intended to talk out these divorce bills. That is not the case, but this is what I do propose to do. I intend to ask that a roll call vote be taken. The many members of this house who on conscientious grounds are opposed to the granting of divorce salve their consciences by having the Speaker repeat, when the motion is carried, " On division."
I intend to make that a reality and to insist on a division being caMed, and then those members who are opposed to divorce, if they are in. earnest, will get up and say so and take the responsibility of that divorce not being granted. As things now stand, upon some of us who are in favour of granting divorce under certain circumstances is thrown the responsibility of divorce not being granted.
I do not think that is fair. I would say, let that responsibility be assumed by those who on conscientious grounds say that under no circumstances should divorce be granted.
I admit that I am somewhat at a loss to know whether to vote in favour of or against these divorces. I would say that I could 
justify my action in either case because I am opposed to this manner of granting divorces by this parliament, but I am not opposed under certain circumstances to the granting of divorces. I think on the whole that probably the way in which I can best express my own position in this matter will be for me to vote against the granting of these divorces, and that for two reasons. I want this to be clearly understood:	First,
that I know nothing whatever about the merits of the individual cases; and knowing nothing of those merits, in voting for them I am as I have said, simply a sort of rubber stamp. Secondly, I vote against them mainly on the ground that I want this to be a protest against this manner of granting divorce. It may be that if I knew the merits of this particular case under discussion I would vote in favour of the bill; but I do not know the merits, and therefore I am quite clear that I ought to vote against it.
However, I would say there may be exceptions to that course of action, and I want to leave myself free as to this. One day, desirous of observing personally the procedure in the senate divorce committee, I sat through the hearing of one entire case. If I can locate that case in the mass of these divorce bills I intend to vote in its favour, because I think the poor woman who sought divorce absolutely deserves it. Having a knowledge of that particular case I would make an exception of it, just as I might have to make an exception of other cases, if in committee their merits are demonstrated. This may not appear entirely consistent: I admit it. But on the whole in taking this attitude of opposition, I want it to be clearly understood that I do so, not because in my judgment there is necessarily anything wrong about granting a divorce in the particular case that comes before us, but primarily because I want to protest against this procedure.
I feel very sorry indeed that in some of these cases to which we are objecting the parties may be put to unnecessary expense and hardship and delay; I feel very sorry for the individuals. On the other hand, I would say that those responsible for this condition of affairs are the people who year after year and year after year refuse to provide proper courts where these matters can be dealt with.
Further, Mr. Speaker, I shall be very sorry unnecessarily to delay the house. I do not think any of us want to prolong the session. But in my view the responsibility for such delay does not rest on those who insist upon giving reality to the proceedings of this house; it rests rather upon those who, ever since I

Procedure respecting Divorce
have been a member of parliament, have refused frankly to face the issues involved in these cases that come to us in such large numbers.

Mr. Speaker, last year this same question was before parliament, and was discussed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) pretty much as he has discussed it to-day. On that occasion I was in entire agreement with him, as I am to-day. I think he has admirably covered the whole situation, and there is very little to be added; but I wish to make dear, as he has done, that while I am glad to have the opportunity to vote against every divorce bill which comes before this house, I do so exactly for the reason that he has pointed out, not that I am opposed under certain circumstances to the granting of divorce, but that I am opposed to this house doing so.
That is, I am opposed to the absurd procedure which year after year is followed in this house. The absurdity cannot be made any more evident than it is at this time. If we were actually to take a vote on the approximately three hundred divorce bills which will be presented to the house this session, provided that the senate committee can hear that many cases, it would hold us here for several months. In order to dispose of them we put them through their various stages like frozen corn is put through a chopping mill- we do not even take time to read the bills, wo call them by number; and we do not even stand up to record our votes-we vote in silence. This procedure appears to me to be absurd. In this house we have no facilities for discovering the true facts in respect to any one of these bills.
What about the senate committee?

I was going to mention
that. I have a great deal of respect for the divorce committee of the senate. I believe it works very hard and very conscientiously, but that does not relieve this house of its responsibilities. How does my hon. friend know that the senate committee has done justice, for instance, in this particular case? I have as much faith in that committee as he has, but I am not going to have its members think for me; he can have them do that for him if :he wishes. No senate committee is going to think for me, even if it can do it better than I can myself. If I am to vote on these bills I want to know what led to the conclusions drawn by the senate committee; like my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, I want to know what is going to become of the children; like him, I want to know what is going to become of those people who are given the right to marry again, which in some cases may mean our permitting the commission of a social crime. I refuse to be a party to that sort of thing.
And I am opposed to this procedure because it has 'become a real problem for the senate. The senate divorce committee is overworked. In fact, I understand that a second committee has had to be appointed to deal with these cases. The senate has protested against this condition of affairs, and it gave point to its protest by sending to this house a bill to establish a divorce court in Ontario. This house refused to endorse the bill, which would have provided a properly constituted court to deal with these cases the majority of which come from this province. So while the senate divorce committee may be perfectly efficient in dealing with these cases, in the first place, it is overworked; in the second place, even although it were all the time efficient in its work, it cannot take the place of this house; we have no right to rely on it to do our business for us.
I think it is only fair to point out Mr. Speaker, that there are but two provinces from which petitions for divorce come to parliament, Ontario and Quebec.
Practically one.

I am corrected by my hon.
friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa): he says " Practically one." Perhaps the Minister of Justice will permit me to refer to the bill which was discussed in this house merely to point out that some of the leading members from both these provinces were most active in its defeat. I think the hon. member for Labelle pointed out that to pass the bill would be to press upon the people of Ontario something that they did not want; and I think his point was well taken. But are we not pressing upon the people of this province something that they do not want when we continue granting divorces that hon. members from that province protest they do not want? So I for one am not going to embarrass those hon. Canutes who strove to stem the tide of divorce by opposing the bill to which I have referred, and by refusing to vote bills of divorce for their constituents. I want them to-day to take the responsibility which they did not take the other day. So far as I am concerned, I am not going to sit mum and be counted as voting for divorce bills that I do not know anything about, and that I do not want or care to know anything about. On the other hand, hon. members whose constituents want divorce, and who make long platitudinous speeches about the
Procedure respecting Divorce

honour and sanctity of the home, which they say I want to destroy by establishing a divorce court for Ontario, will not now be able to sit silent while their bills are going through this house.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to repeat what I said at the beginning, that I am not unfavourable to granting divorce under certain circumstances. I deeply deplore the principle on which divorces are granted, even in our courts to-day, and as they are granted in this parliament. I hope if we are going to continue to grant divorce, the evidence will have to be based on the unhappiness of the people concerned, and not on the filth which fills these reports to-day. That is the ground upon which I should like to see divorce granted, if it is granted at all. I am opposed to any single case that is before parliament. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, I do not know what are the merits of any individual case, and therefore I am not in a position to vote for an3' particular bill. I can only vote against these divorce bills in the hope that ultimately these cases will be dealt with by a properly constituted court. I am glad to have this opportunity of voting against every divorce bill that comes before this house.

In the long period during which I have been a member of this house I have consistently opposed the granting of divorce, and in those thirty years no application has come from my constituency for a dissolution of marriage. I am not objecting to this bill in particular; I am objecting to the principle of the bill. We spend days and nights, weeks and months, years and decades in discussing the material interests of the people, discussing our railway situation, our tariff, our finances, everything that concerns the wealth and prosperity of the country. But how much time do we devote to protecting the home and the generation that is to come afterwards? Grave mistakes have been committed on this question of divorce, and to begin the argument I wish to lay before the house I shall cite the opinion of the outstanding statesman whom Canada had produced up to confederation, the father of confederation'-Sir John A. Macdonald- who declared that in 1857, when the British parliament enacted the divorce law there, it committed a serious blunder. I wish to read these words from Sir John because I know they will have some weight in this house and in this country. This is what he said:
I am convinced that the establishment of a divorce court_ in England has been productive of much mischief. In former times, the procedure with respect to divorce was the same as in force in Canada to-day-that is, it could

only be obtained from the upper house of parliament. In those days divorces were rare, expensive and hard to get, and the morals of the community were spared the columns of scandal with which the English papers are occasionally filled. The establishment of the divorce court in Canada would mean cheap and easy divorces, which would lead to great laxity in the marriage relations. They are beginning to see that in the old country. I hope it may be long before we have anything of the kind in Canada.
What year was that?

I have not the exact year
in which these words were uttered, but evidently it was after confederation. The British parliament has enacted within the last two or three years a measure to prohibit the publication in English papers of columns upon columns of Scandal which were perverting and demoralizing the youth of that country. We publish such matter now in the evidence which is taken in such cases and circulated through these corridors, and which finds its way among young people who should never read it. Unfortunately the thing is going from bad to worse.
I have given the opinion of Sir John Macdonald with reference to a previous generation; let me now give the opinion of another outstanding Canadian, one of the sons of Ontario, who commands the respect of this house and is now Chief Justice of that province. Sir W'illiam Mulock has said:
J think the facility with which divorces are granted in England and in other countries does go a long way to interfere with the sacredness of the marriage tie. There is no reason that justifies, in my opinion, the establishment of a divorce court for the province of Ontario.
Such were the opinions expressed by men who command the respect of the Canadian people, and I have no hesitation in saying that, no matter to what religion people may belong, the immense majority of the Canadian people, 95 per cent of them, still want the home preserved and the marriage tie respected. We are a Christian country, thank God. Canada is surely not going to follow in the footsteps of our neighbours to the south, where the marriage relation has fallen so low-the lowest in the scale of all great nations. Statistics speak. Let us look back and se'e what happened when divorce was imposed upon us. We know how it came about; after the adoption of the divorce law in England in 1857 Nova Scotia and New Brunswick established divorce courts. Prince Edward Island never took advantage of that law; and let it be said to the honour of that province that to-day it is the only province in the Dominion in which but one divorce has been granted since 1867. What has been the

Procedure Respecting Divorce
result of the institution of divorce in Canada? When the question of divorce came before the fathers of confederation, Sir Hector Langevin, speaking for the government of that day, said:
Let us now examine the question of divorce. We do not intend either to establish or to recognize a new right, we do not mean to admit a thing to which we have constantly refused to assent. But at the conference the question arose which legislature should exercise the different powers which already exist in the constitutions of the different provinces. Now, among those powers which have been already and frequently exercised de facto, is that of divorce. As a member of the conference, without admitting or creating any new right in this behalf and while declaring, as I now do, that as Catholics we acknowledge no power of divorce, I found that we were to decide in what legislative body the authority should be lodged which we found in our constitutions. After mature consideration, we resolved to leave it to the central legislature, thinking thereby to increase the difficulties of procedure which is at present so easy.
We found this power existing in the constitutions of the different provinces and not being able to get rid of it, we wished to banish it as far from us as possible.
What has been the record since confederation? In the first decade, from 1867 to 1877, 7 divorces were granted. From 1877-87, there were 16; 1887-97, 36; 1897-1907, 53; 1907-17, over 200; 1917-27, 1,070; and in 1928 alone parliament granted 238. So that the total number of divorces granted by parliament in that period was 1,620, for the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. And the total for the whole of Canada from 1913 to 1928 was 6,052.
There are in this house fathers of families, men who will be responsible to another generation for what we do here; and our records will stand up against them. Are we doing what we should do now to safeguard the sanctity of the home and to render marriage indestructible, or are we not rather going about it in a slipshod manner, allowing divorces to be granted automatically by a few senators on the other side? Indeed, we go so far as to lump them together and pass them en bloc. Surely that is not the sort of legislation which this parliament should give to the Canadian people. This is a serious, a grave question; it is not a party question. The responsibility lies on all sides and on all members of the house. I know the present government will have to consider the question because we cannot allow the present state of things to continue. Some means will have to be found to change the present situation.
I want to give another illustration of what has taken place as a result of the legislation passed in this house whereby the provinces in the west were allowed to introduceinto Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba- the English law in respect to this matter. In the short time at my disposal I have no opportunity to discuss the attitude of the Roman Catholic church in this regard. That church is the mother church of all Christianity; it was the church of all Christians for fifteen hundred years and it always stood for the teachings of Christ as it understood them. Since then there have been changes; Christians do not agree upon the interpretation of certain passages in St. Matthew, but surely no man in this house to-day would pretend for one moment that our Lord and Master declared that a divorced person could marry again within the lifetime oif the other party.
I hold in my hand a 'book entitled Divorce in America, which contains an introduction by the Right Reverend William T. Manning, Bishop of New York, in which he describes in a few words the horrible condition now prevailing in the United States. Are we to follow in the footsteps of that country, where the people themselves are trying to have the marriage tie respected and the homes saved? After referring to the enormous increase in the divorces granted in the United States, where the average is one divorce in five marriages; after calling attention to the fact that fifty-two different reasons are given for the granting of divorce, and after stating that divorces granted in one state are not recognized in another, this Episcopalian bishop says:
It is our duty to face this situation, to consider its causes and its consequences, and to ask ourselves how it can best be remedied.
The separation of man and wife, and their living apart, for grave cause, is not forbidden by the church. The church allows, and in extreme cases even advises this. It is the use
