Mr. Speaker,
I do not apprehend that this is the time or place to discuss the principle underlying divorce; the fact of the matter is that we have divorce in Canada and that this parliament has been charged under the British North America Act with the responsibility of granting divorce. That is the situation prevailing to-day, whether we like it or not.
I am quite well aware that it is not in order to reflect upon a bill which has been presented to the house already during this session or upon a vote which has been taken here, but

Procedure Respecting Divorce
I will say that I believe those who have brought this matter before the house have done a service in that they have shown the absurdity of the position taken by the house on a former occasion this session. We are not discussing the theory of divorce; we are face to face with certain conditions, and I think it was because the house failed to realize that fact that we acted as we did a few weeks ago. That is all I wish to say upon that point because, as I have stated, I am well aware that it is not in order to discuss a question which has been before the house already or a vote which was taken on a previous occasion. The question which confronts us now is this: a large number of divorce bills have come before this chamber during a long period of .years; how we shall conduct ourselves with regard to that condition? The hon. member who introduced this matter has rendered a service to the house, in that he has placed before us the condition which exists. I cannot follow him, or the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine), who supported him, to the extent of going as far as they have gone. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) stated that he proposed to vote against this bill because he did not know anything about it; the hon. member for Wetaskiwin said that he would vote against these bills because he did not know the particulars and did not wish to know them. I would say to the hon. members that they are negligent in their duty in that regard. I am not saying that I am better informed than they are with regard to this particular bill, but when they advance that as the reason for their action, then I say to that extent they are negligent in their duty. They say that they do not propose to discharge their duty as members of parliament because they have not informed themselves on the question before the house.
Has the hon. member read the evidence relating to this case?

I have already confessed
that I have not read the evidence, but I do not propose to make that an excuse for not doing my duty.

On what ground
does the hon. member propose to support the bill?

Mr. Speaker, I quite agree with the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Brown) when he says that this is not the proper time to discuss the broad issue of the principle of divorce. I also agree with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) when he says that it is not in order to discuss the question of the establishment of divorce courts because, as he says, that question has been decided, for this year at least, by a vote of the house. At the same time, I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has justified the course he has taken when he points out, by way of exemplification, the consequence of the attitude taken by the house on a previous occasion. I think we are all agreed that the hon. member for Lisgar is a very sensible man. He said that he did not want to discuss the theory; he admitted that the system was bad, but he wanted to deal with the system as it is. Carried to its logical conclusion, the position taken by the hon. gentleman would only mean that every time the house found that something was wrong, it could do nothing to remedy the condition complained of because of its being the system then in effect.
No, no.

Fortunately, parliaments very seldom act logically.

Procedure Respecting Divorce

He wanted to point out
that a mistake had been made on a previous vote.

I would advise the hon. minister, who is a canny Scotchman, not to come to the rescue of the hon. member for Lisgar, who is just as canny a Scotchman as he is.
In connecting the words of the hon. member for Lisgar with those of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, my construction is that this parliament is not empowered to deal with the civil rights when it grants a divorce; that it is not empowered to deal with property belonging to the divorced parties or to the children; that it is not empowered to decide what shall be granted to the divorced party who may be in the right in asking for the divorce, or to his or her children. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think the point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in connection with this bill, and all similar ones, is very well taken. The point raised that under subsection 26 of clause 91 of the British North America Act we are dealing with questions upon which we have no power to pass final judgment and do justice to all parties, is a very grave constitutional point.
No power to grant money or alimony.

Of course not. It may have been done in one case or another, but many things are done occasionally by parliament. or occasionally by a provincial legislature which are against the letter of the constitution. Such a thing stands so long as it is not challenged, but look at what it means. It means that things are done haphazardly which may be challenged ten or fifteen years later in a court of justice and upon which the Supreme- Court of Canada or the Privy Council will pass final judgment, doing away with the whole of our jurisprudence. I do not want to go too much outside this debate, but this has happened with regard to mariage jurisprudence in Quebec. Year after year the superior court, the court of review and the court of appeal of Quebec rendered judgments in a certain sense, when all of a sudden, in the year of grace 1921, the Privy Council gave what some consider as a judgment but what others merely call an opinion, which has practically upset the whole of our jurisprudence in Quebec since confederation. The more I have studied the question-and I have given a good deal of time to it-the more I have become convinced that that judgment of the Privy Council is. legally speaking, the right one. But what does it mean? That for
[Mr. Bourassa.?
years and years the legislature of Quebec and the tribunals of that province acted upon a delusion which that final judgment of the Privy Council simply dispelled. So much for the constitutional issue.
Are we going to take the position that, because certain things have been done for ten, twenty-five or thirty years, we are to go on doing the same? Let us carry that also to its logical conclusion. Let us apply it to any principle or practice of policy in connection with public affairs or private interest. Are we going to consider ourselves bound by what has been done from year to year or from decade to decade by the house or by the senate? Is so, why have a parliament? Why not adopt a final act of (parliament in the form and terms of the laws of -the Medes and Persians and say that what is law shall be law for all time to come?
We have that under the British North America Act.

That some old-time
Tories who no longer exist even in this house, should have upheld the principle that certain laws or practices should always remain unaltered, I can understand; but that any man, calling himself Liberal, Progressive or Liberal-Conservative, should stand up in the house and say: I will not consider the- merits of a concrete issue, or I will not consider the principle of a certain form of legislation, because it depends upon a system which has -been practised for fifty years, is something I cannot understand. For my part I do not think I was elected in the year of grace 1926 by a portion of the Canadian electorate to come here and do something because it had been done from session to session for the last fifty years.
To apply those considerations to the question at issue, I said before, and I repeat now-

I rise to a point of order.
This is a bill before the house and the hon. member is not discussing the merits or demerits of it. He is discussing the principle whether parliament should deal with such bills or not. That matteT has been dealt with already by the house at this session, and I submit that the whole discussion is out of order. The only matter which the house can discuss is whether this particular bill is one which should be passed by the house.

Speaking on the point
of order, I quite agree with the hon. gentleman: I think the whole discussion is out of order. But why should the point be raised when I am endeavouring to clear up the issue brought before the house by three hon. members who preceded me?

Procedure Respecting Divorce
The hon. member is now applying the principle he has just condemned.

Quite so. I prefaced it
by saying that logic had nothing to do with our procedure.

The question before the
house is the second reading of a particular bill in regard to divorce. It is very hard to make a distinction between the principle contained in that bill and the general principle of divorce; but as the hon. member for La-belle admits that he is out of order, I hope he will confine his remarks to the particular subject before the house. I repeat, however, it is very difficult to establish a distinction between the principle of divorce that obtains in this particular bill and the general principle itself.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, because that will cut short the discussion, and I hope the decision will stand against further speeches.
With regard to this particular bill, it is a divorce bill. It is a divorce bill framed in the same language as that in which all divorce bills are framed, adopted by the senate and brought before the house. If you go through the statutes of the last fifty years or about so, you find that every divorce granted by parliament, for whatever reasons or causes, is granted in the same form. There is a printed formula in both languages, French and English, and there are blank spaces for the name, the date, the date of the marriage, the date, I think, at which the case has been brought before the senate, or something to that effect. A few words are filled in and the form is adopted by a committee of the senate, sent to this house and passed upon by us without our reading the evidence. I think that will be admitted by every fair-minded man. At least nineteen out of twenty members do not read the evidence; at any rate they do not read the evidence of all those bills, so that, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. WToodsworth) has said, we act as rubber stamps in order to ratify what has been done by the senate committee under those conditions. I claim that is a bad system of legislation.
With regard to this particular bill we have to look first to the principle upon which it is based. We have to consider the principle upon which we act upon this bill or any other similar piece of legislation. Are we acting as a sovereign parliament, as a branch of this sovereign parliament equal in power to and exercising the same responsibilities as the other branch, or are we acting as a court
of justice? It is one or the other, or both, perhaps. Under subsection 26 of section 91 of the British North America Act, parliament has the sole and exclusive power to deal with marriage and divorce, either from a legislative or from a legal point of view. In other words, no divorce can be granted except by leave of this parliament, directly through private bills as is the case now, or indirectly through the decisions of courts of justice empowered by parliament to act in this regard, with the exception of those courts of divorce which existed in the maritime provinces prior to confederation. Let there be no mistake: the divorce courts that have been established and are working now in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, have been established and are adjudicating under the authority of parliament, under the authority of law passed by parliament
With regard to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, which had no divorce courts prior to Confederation, and in which this parliament has not thought proper to establish divorce courts, this parliament acts directly upon every divorce bill, first as a legislative power, and second as a court of justice. It is a great axiom of British jurisprudence that where a right is created by parliament, rightly or wrongly, some court of justice must exist to adjudicate upon the concrete issues which are raised in connection with that right. I think that has been an uncontradicted principle of British government, British legislation and British jurisprudence for centuries past. Therefore, this parliament having received from the British parliament, at its own request, the exclusive power to legislate on marriage and divorce, it has taken a moral or an immoral pledge towards people who believe in divorce to give them a means to exercise that right, which I consider a contradiction of social right and social duty, but of which nevertheless this parliament has accepted the responsibility.

Does the hon. member
mean to say that under subsection 26 of section 91 of the British North America Act this parliament is bound to act on matters of divorce when it is applied to?

That is the construction I put upon that principle of British jurisprudence, that where there is a right there must be an adjudication upon issues in connection with that right by some form of tribunal. I think that is contained in our code of civil procedure in the province of Quebec as one of its first principles. I am not a lawyeri 578

Procedure Respecting Divorce
It is elementary law anyway.

Of course. How can a
parliament which in the name of the sovereign exercises all powers of legislation without limitation, including the creation of courts of adjudication, claim to itself and have put into its national charter the exclusive power to deal on certain subjects unless it is prepared to grant to every citizen of the country a recourse to see whether or not he has the right to invoke that principle of law? It is for that reason that I repeat to-day what I have always said that the one great moral and social crime of the fathers of confederation was to introduce the principle of divorce into the constitution.
I come back to this bill, and my remarks will apply to the next bill and to all these other bills. I cannot understand how anyone who is opposed to divorce on principle, who believes that divorce is wrong morally and socially, can vote for any one of these divorce bills that are brought before parliament. You may say that I have done it. Yes, in a way. We all well know that all of us have done things that had better not have been done. Let us have a little humility. All of us in the course of our political lives have done things which we would like not to have done; but am I to be told in this year 1929, when age is coming upon me, that because I have been wrong or unthoughtful for many years, I am now precluded from being a little more thoughtful and thinking more of my responsibilities to my God, to my country, to my own children and to the children of others? If I have been lightheaded and unreflective in letting pass for years bills of divorce, "carried on division," I am not going to do so in the future. I said last year and I repeat it now-not in any spirit of enmity to this house, to any party in this house or to any individual- the more I grow in age, the more I reflect upon the evolutions of human society, and the more I am convinced that the canker-worm which is eating into the entrails of modern nations is, as the hon. member for Bona venture (Mr. Marcil) has said, the destruction of the sanctity of the home.
Reference has been made to individual sufferings, to the men and women who occasionally are victims of a bad marriage. But can you point to one single law which does not carry with it some individual suffering? Can you point to one single law upon which society rests, and upon which rests the magnificent political fabric of which we are so proud, which has not multiplied martyrs all through 
the centuries of the glorious history of the British Empire, and of the world at large? No. When it comes to the foundations of society you have to choose between social principles upon which no concessions should be made, in regard to which no transactions should be consented to, and the suffering of some few individuals.
As to those who do not agree with me on this point,, I respect their views. But if they think as does the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and apparently the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) although he was not as clear, if they admit that on certain occasions and for certain causes divorce ought to be granted, then I come back to the other point, that such action should >be taken in a judicial manner, and divorce should never be granted unless all the rules of equity and justice and evidence are applied to each case.
Why did you not vote that way when the bill was before the house?

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. The hon. gentleman does not have to, of course, but if he had listened to me or had read my speech, I am sure that with his keen mind he would see that I am taking now exactly the same position that I took last year, and this year again.
There is the record of your vote.

I voted against the
establishment of divorce courts by this parliament, after I had put to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre the question, "Are you prepared to amend your bill by introducing into it a clause saying that any divorce court established in any province of Canada shall not come into existence before t'he people of that particular community shall have expressed their will in favour of it?" That is exactly my stand to-day.
When my hon. friend interrupted I was going on to make this point. As regards those members of this house who are opposed to divorce on principle, whether you call it religious principle, social principle or political principle, I do not see 'how they can go on voting for all these divorce bills, and for my part I propose to vote against every one of them every time it is possible to get a division in the house. As to those who think it is their right and their duty to look into the merits of each case, then it comes to a question of their exercising judicial duties. It is admitted that divorce cases are coming to this parliament only from those provinces in which there are no divorce courts. As a

Procedure Respecting Divorce
matter of fact, as I pointed out to the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine), they are practically all coming from Ontario. This parliament, therefore, having taken upon itself the responsibility of acting as a divorce court for the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec, I claim that those hon. members who are of the opinion that each case should be decided on its merits must hold the view that 'both branches of this parliament should make full use of all their powers of inquiry before any divorce bill is granted, just as a court of justice would do before giving the decision of the court in favour of this, that or the other party. You must aipply all the rules of evidence that are in force in all these courts [DOT]which this parliament has created, whether it be the supreme court, the exchequer court or any other court which has been created either by this parliament or by the legislatures of the various provinces, some under their own authority, and others, such as the Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba divorce courts, under the authority of this parliament. You must see that the truth is vindicated as far as you can vindicate it. You must see that the principles of equity and social justice are applied to all parties.
One hon. gentleman, I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, told of a correspondence he had last year with regard to one of those divorce cases. I also had letters from one of the leading legal offices in Toronto pointing out to me the abominable injustice that was done in a certain case. Whether it was true or not, I do not know, I had no power to inquire into the matter. But it turned out that the senate committee ruled that it had no power either, or did not choose to exercise such power if it had any. Thereupon the woman protested that being too poor to come here to vindicate her honour, a gross injustice had been done to her, that her life had been broken by a decision of parliament which precluded her from being heard. The senate committee passed judgment upon the case; this house passed, not judgment, but ratified the decision of the divorce committee of the senate apparently for the reason-surprising to me-that we have such confidence in one committee of one branch of this parliament that we renounce our responsibilities, we put our conscience, our intelligence and our will into the hands of the eight or ten gentlemen composing that committee. Capable as they may be, learned as they may be, I am not prepared to say, Mr. Speaker, and I do not think I could justify myself before the people who have sent me here by saying: I may have done wrong, I may have been ^a party to a
mistaken decision by the senate committee, but the case was in the hands of that committee, and although the bill could not pass without my vote, I gave my vote without inquiry, blindly, and without knowing anything of the circumstances, because I had confidence in those gentlemen. I cannot agree to do any such thing.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, opposed as I am to divorce in principle, whatever reasons may be advanced in favour of it, believing that marriage is essentially a social principle before it is a question of contract or civil rights, believing, apart from the individual suffering that may arise from the maintenance of any particular marriage, that the great interests of society at large require the maintenance of the natural law and of the evangelical doctrine based upon it and sanctified by the word of Christ, that a marriage once contracted is contracted for life, I propose to vote against every divorce bill. In the next place, not believing that under the present system I can properly exercise those powers of judicial inquiry and judgment which we are called upon to exercise in these matters, I do nob propose to sit as one of the judges on any divorce case; consequently I rule the case out of court by the only means I have at my command, and that is by voting against this bill, against the next bill, and against every other divorce bill 'that may come before this parliament.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am as desirous of
preserving the sanctity of marriage and of married life as any member of this house could be. I was born and bred and I practised in the early years of my profession in the province of Nova Scotia, where we had a divorce court prior to confederation, a court which still continues to function. On that court sit judges appointed from time to time, both of Roman Catholic and the Anglican faith, who in their inmost hearts are opposed to the principle of divorce. And I presume that every judge finds the duty imposed upon him from time to time of administering laws to which he may be in principle opposed, and, if he were a member of the legislative assembly or parliament upon whom the responsibility is placed of enacting those laws, he would have voted on principle against their enactment. But the judges of that court find themselves in this judicial position, that they are bound by the solemn oath of office to administer the law which comes before them, although they are not morally or personally responsible for enactment of the law. Their sole duty is to pronounce a decision in accordance with the law which is then being administered by the

Procedure Respecting Divorce
court. It is in a similar position that I sit here as one of the members of the high court of parliament of Canada.
The constitution of this country has placed the duty and the responsibility upon the members of this house of administering and carrying out the purpose and intent of that constitution as expressed in the British North America Act. Section 91 declares:
It shall be lawful for the queen, by and with the advice and consent of the senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order, and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces; and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms of this section, it is hereby declared that (notwithstanding anything in this act) the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated, that is to say,-
And number 26 is:
Marriage and divorce.
In respect of marriage and divorce parliament sits as a high court, both the commons and the senate. In times past it has been the custom for these divorce bills to be introduced in the senate and thoroughly investigated by a committee of the senate-I presume because that chamber has more time at its disposal- and the pronouncement of the senate committee has generally been accepted by this house. So long as that judicial function is imposed upon parliament, I regard it as my bounden duty to vote on the merits of each divorce bill that is brought before this house. I confess, as hon. members have stated this afternoon, that it is impossible for me to give adequate consideration to the evidence in each case which is printed by the senate committee and sent to every member of this house. I feel reluctant, really, to devote the time necessary to reading that evidence. Occasionally I have taken up at random the evidence in connection with some divorce bill and in the majority of cases, under the law which prevails in this country, I consider the applicants entitled to divorce. In other cases, not having heard the evidence, and perhaps construing it differently from those who heard it orally -because there is a great difference in my experience between reading the printed report of evidence and hearing the witnesses as they give that evidence before the committee-I should be doubtful whether I, sitting as a member of the committee ini such cases, looking at the evidence as it is printed1 and not having heard it, would have rendered the same decision as that rendered by the senate committee. Therefore I have felt that it would be far

better for parliament, and far better for the country, to impose on one of the courts of justice of the land the consideration of these petitions for divorce; because I believe that the judges of this country are far better qualified to render decisions in such cases than are we as members of the high court of parliament. But parliament in its wisdom has decided against relegating this judicial duty to the courts of the province of Ontario, and therefore so long as these bills from Ontario, relating to that province particularly, come before this parliament I feel in duty bound, under my responsibility as a member of this parliament, which is the high court of justice in Canada, to determine according to my conscience and according to the evidence given as to whether I will vote in favour of or oppose each particular bill which is brought before the house. It is very difficult, I repeat, for one to perform in this house that conscientious duty; but under the constitution of the country I think the duty is imposed upon us until such time as parliament decides in its wisdom to relegate that duty to the courts of justice. The divorce court-in the English-speaking provinces which have such courts-not only grants divorces on certain grounds of which we are all aware, but also nullifies marriages which have not been contracted according to the law. In the province of Quebec our courts exercise that jurisdiction of nullifying marriage contracts under certain circumstances, and that to a certain extent relieves those who are domiciled in Quebec from making application for divorce to the parliament of Canada. In the province of Ontario, so far, it appears that there is no consensus of opinion on the part of members representing that province as to whether divorce proceedings are better administered by this high court of parliament or would be better administered by the courts of Ontario. I have no doubt as to that; I think divorce should be relegated to those courts. And as regards the province of Quebec, with all due consideration for the views of my hon. colleagues from that province, whose religious convictions I understand and appreciate, and whose conscientious objections to divorce I also thoroughly understand and appreciate, I say that my own personal opinion is that it would be far better that the duty should be relegated to the courts of justice in that province, and that fewer mistakes would be made in administering the law if its administration were within the jurisdiction of its provincial courts.

Knowing the sentiment of Quebec as he knows it, and knowing that the

Procedure Respecting Divorce
immense majority of the people inhabiting that province are opposed to divorce, would my bon. friend undertake to impose it on the province ?

No, I certainly would not; because many policies which, iln principle both my hon. friend and I might advocate, are nevertheless inexpedient, if it is suggested that we apply them to the whole Dominion generally. Therefore I should be opposed to imposing the administration of divorce upon the province of Quebec so Long as it objected to divorce. And in the same way I would oppose-at least I would not favour -the imposition of the administration of divorce upon the courts of Ontario so long as there is any strong public opinion against it in that province. That is my position.
I think that we are above ordinary sectarian prejudices in this high court; and as, one who has a sincere respect for the religious convictions of his fellow men, I therefore, would not impose upon any province the administration of a law, which was not acceptable to that province, either in respect of marriage or in respect of divorce. But, so long as the constitution of this country remains as it is, I feel it is my duty to give a judicial decision in respect of every petition for divorce that comes properly before this house and this parliament. So that irrespective of my own personal views with regard to divorce-and, I repeat, I believe in the sanctity of the marriage relation as deeply and sincerely as my hon. colleagues from the province of Quebec-I say that so long as the duty is imposed upon me by the constitution of this country, I feel I must administer the law, whatever my personal prede-lictions may be. It may be very distasteful to me, and in many cases it may not be in accordance with what I think should be accepted as the better way of administering the law. , Therefore, so far as this bill is concerned, on which apparently the evidence is conclusive, holding these opinions, I regard myself as in just the same position as a judge of the court of Nova Scotia, of the Catholic faith, who would feel, when the evidence was brought before him, that it was his duty and responsibility to administer the law in accordance with that evidence, although the principle of granting divorces might be utterly distasteful to him. That is the position which I intend to take in this house. So far as the province of Ontario is concerned I see no hope of relegating the duty of administering the law of divorce to the judiciary of that province, until the province actually requests it so clearly as to persuade us to legislate accordingly. At the same time I may add
that so long as we sit as a high court of parliament, exercising judicial functions, I hope I may have sufficient moral strength and personal courage to administer the law, even though sometimes I would not favour the enactment of the law under which that administration takes place.

Mr. Speaker, I have been a member of the House of Commons for a good many years and I have heard the question of divorce discussed on many occasions. I venture to say that no member of this house is more opposed to divorce on conscientious grounds than I am, because I believe a man and wife contracted to live together and that no legislative body has the right to dissolve that contract.
I ha%re attended only one divorce court in my life, and to me it was a pathetic scene. The husband, a young man of fine appearance, brought charges against his wife, who was present in the court, and during the progress of the case the husband brought out what his six year old boy had said with regard to what he had seen his mother do. This young man seemed quite prosperous and bad given his wife valuable rings and other jewellery; in fact he was so devoted that he deeded his home and made over stocks to her. During the progress of the case the husband charged that the wife drank champagne, scotch and other liquors and went about the country with other men; later I heard the wife say that her husband was a drunken creature, and so on. Each had had an illness, and each claimed that during those illnesses the other had been untrue. It was very pathetic to think that the husband would not attend to his sick wife or that the wife, while her husband was ill, went around the country with other men drinking intoxicating liquor. If I had been given an opportunity to speak to those people I believe I could have brought about a reconciliation, because in the United States I have known of people being separated and then remarrying after having been brought together again by their children or by friends.
I can remember when, so far as I knew, there was not a divorce court in the United States. Now they are located everywhere, and some of the wealthiest women take their children to those nasty places to listen to this terrible evidence. In the United States there are over fifty grounds for divorce; they even grant divorce in some states for incompatibility of temperament. In my opinion divorce is a cancer which eventually will destroy any country; many of the best thinking people of the United States say that divorce will bring about the downfall of that great country. In Canada we can boast of a virile people; we

Procedure Respecting Divorce
are a great nation, recognizing all the moral laws and the laws of God, but as the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) has stated, divorces have increased in Canada from only seven in one year to about two thousand, and every divorce means broken hearts. If the parties to the divorce do not suffer so much their relatives and their children are disgraced and1 shamed. Our homes are the bulwarks of our nation, and when we destroy the homes we weaken the moral fibre of our Canadian people. So when we grant divorces we take a tremendous responsibility upon our shoulders.
As a member of parliament I have been accused of assisting to procure divorces. No member of this house assists in that way; divorces are railroaded through the house and we must acce.pt the responsibility. I want it distinctly understood that I will oppose in every way any divorce law or measure which may be brought up an this house at any time. What an example we are setting the rising generation, the children who are the hope of the world for the future. We should picture the broken homes, the broken hearts, the disappointed fathers, mothers, sisters and brothers when we consider the question of divorce.
I am not speaking from the constitutional standpoint, which was dealt with by the speaker who preceded me; I believe divorce is destroying our nation, and if this parliament accepts responsibility for aiding and abetting such conditions, I propose to make my stand known. I have not read the evidence in a divorce case for over five years; when these reports come to me I tear them up, and I tried to burn them but I could not do so.
There was one case of divorce in my county and not more than a dozen words appeared in the reports in relation to this case. The man had deserted his wife when the children were quite small. When the children were about twenty-one years of age, the wife finally located him. She, with her sister, discovered him living with another woman in the state of "Vermont. There were four children and the wife was told that her husband was the father of those children, which he acknowledged in the presence of his wife and her sister. That is all that would be required to be proved in order to obtain a divorce. The granting of divorces will increase in number because a contaminated thing grows fast, and it would be a terrible misfortune for the youth of this country should they come to realize that members of parliament would support legislation that would destroy the sanctity of the home.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to say any-
thing on this question, but I would like to call the attention of the house to the matter under consideration. This is the second reading of Bill No. 85, letter E of the senate. By saying yes or no with regard to the second reading of this bill, we either register our opinion in favour of advancing the bill one stage, or register our opinion against such advancement. In order to give my own personal opinion, I might say that I am not opposed to the entire bill. I might go further and say that I am not absolutely opposed to the granting of divorces, but I am opposed to certain portions of the bill now before us. We find the bill divided into three parts, the first of which is the preamble. The preamble reads:
Whereas Effie Margaret Hill, residing at the city of Chatham, in the province of Ontario, factory worker, wife of Charles Henry Hill, clock repairer, who is domiciled in Canada and residing at the city of London, in the said province, has by her petition alleged that they were married on the first day of September, A.D. 1920, at the said city of Chatham, she then being Effie Margaret Borland, a spinster; and whereas by her petition she has prayed that, because of his adultery since then, their marriage be dissolved; and whereas the said marriage and adultery have been proved by evidence adduced and it is expedient that the
grayer of her petition be granted: Therefore [is Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:-
There is nothing in the preamble which should meet with opposition. We take it for granted that the senate committee has thoroughly considered the evidence adduced, and has come to the conclusion that the adultery has been proven. Relying on the thorough investigation which has been made, I am prepared to agree to the preamble. If adultery has been committed, it is possible that these two parties are not living together, and, therefore, I am quite willing that this part of the bill should pass. Clause 1 of the bill reads as follows:
The said marriage between Effie Margaret Borland and Charles Henry Hill, her husband, is hereby dissolved, and shall be henceforth null and void.
Up to that point I am in favour of that clause, but I would think that the next clause, "to all intents and purposes whatsoever" might be omitted. If something has come between two parties who have been legally married and which prevents them living together, then I have no objection to legislation being passed which will permit them to live apart. I do not claim that it is necessary that they come here to obtain that right, they could go before a court and get a judicial separation. Of course, it is

Procedure Respecting Divorce
not always possible to arrive at an amicable settlement in a court, which I think is necessary in order to have a satisfactory judicial separation. We might have parties coming here and asking for a bill of divorce whereby they could be eternally separated, as the saying goes. The next clause in this bill reads as follows:
2. The said Effie Margaret Borland may at any time hereafter marry any man whom she might lawfully marry if the said marriage with the said Charles Henry Hill had not been solemnized.
I am not prepared to sanction that part of this bill. In giving my reason for arriving at this conclusion I need only say that we have a Book which is used in this so-called Christian land, a Book which is an authority prior to any statute which might be passed by this parliament. In the twentieth chapter of Exodus there are certain commands given to us to obey. One of those commands is, "Thou shalt not steal," and we take it for granted that when people do steal they commit a wrong and we pass laws to bring them to task.

It depends upon the
amount of money they steal.

Without a doubt,
the punishment is according to the offence. Another command in that same chapter is, "Thou shalt not kill." When people go out and violate that command they are punishable by either imprisonment for a term of years, or possibly by death.
Again it depends.

Another command
is, "Thou shalt not commit adultery." The one Person who is partly responsible for that written message in the twentieth chapter of Exodus was here upon earth, and he told us in very plain language-language which I cannot discard or get around in order to explain away-"Whosoever shall marry her that is divorced committeth adultery." How can these injunctions be reconciled with what is proposed here? I cannot reconcile them myself, and, therefore, I refuse to sanction the second clause of this bill. I feel that if we as a parliament sanction such a bill we, in effect, legalize adultery. We override what, to my mind, is a greater authority than any law that we could pass in parliament.

May I suggest,
though, that we have never considered the possibility of bringing in a law against adultery?

Well, that is the
opinion of the hon. member, but-

No, I say that as
a matter of fact, parliament has no law against adultery.

Quite true. We
have laws against stealing; we have laws against killing, and it is quite possible we may advocate a law against adultery. Somebody may be prepared to say that the Founder of the Christian religion more or less sanctioned divorce when He was asked the question in regard to the practice of Moses. I do not believe He did. He was asked: Why did Moses allow divorces in his time? And his answer was that Moses, because of the hardness of their hearts suffered them to give writings of divorcement and to put away their wives, but from the beginning it was not so. That is the attitude I prefer to take, namely, that from the beginning such was not so and was not intended to be so, and I feel that we, in this year of Our Lord, 1929, instead of getting further away from the beginning, should make some attempt to get back to what was the intention in the beginning. Therefore I am going to vote against this bill for the reason that I think the right to marry again should not be included in any of these bills.
Some hon. members have advocated that this matter should come before a court; that the courts are more capable of inquiring into the details and adjudicating upon such matters than we in this house are. I gather that parliament is a court above every other court in the land and we should give the lead as to what course we would expect our courts to follow in similar cases. Our lead should be against passing any bill that gives the right to marry again.
The question was raised whether or not adultery could be made a punishable offence. Why could it not be made an offence? Adultery is taken as the absolute ground for divorce in Canada. If adultery were made a punishable, a statutory offence-and I am not going to suggest to what extent the punishment should be made effective-I am not so sure but that we would curb our divorce evil much more readily than we are doing even by opposing divorce bills. If adultery were made a punishable offence on the part of the person who was the cause of the divorce proceedings, and then if we followed that a little further and classified any person who married after being granted a divorce, as being guilty of adultery and liable to such punishable offence, I am rather of opinion that we would curb our divorce evil to a greater extent. For these various reasons I am going to vote against Bill No. 85, and every other divorce bill that comes before the house.
