The committee can do one of two things: they can call witnesses, hear evidence and determine the action to be taken; or they can do what the probate division does in England, take the depositions already made under oath, read them and determine whether or not the bill shall be accepted.
Now, I wonder if my friend from Wetaskiwin realizes that this parliament consists of two houses, the senate and the commons. A divorce bill is not an act of parliament until it has been approved by both houses. The commons, giving the bill its second reading and referring it to a committee, the committee takes the sworn depositions that were made before the senate committee, and upon reading those depositions it dispenses with the calling of the witnesses. The probate division in England in a very important case involving a question of very serious consequences to the parties engaged, one of *whom lived in Alberta, recently took evidence by affidavit and heard it before Lord1 Merrivale, president of the court, rather than take the witnesses across the Atlantic ocean to testify. And this house in sending a divorce bill to a committee does not ask that committee to deal with it in any particular way; it leaves it open for the committee to take its own course. For instance, if the member for Wetaskiwin so desires, he may say: We will put these people to all the expense and trouble of calling witnesses before our committee. Or committee may proceed as the British courts of justice have proceeded for many years in admiralty cases, in divorce cases, and in cases in the chancery and king's bench divisions, read, if it is thought desirable, evidence already taken before a committee of another house under oath-upon which perjury might be charged-for the purpose of
satisfying itself-the committee-that the
case alleged against the defendant has been made out. Now, is it possible that this House of Commons desires so to hold up to the world-shall I say?-our inability to grapple with a simple problem by making it appear, as my friend from Winnipeg North

Procedure Respecting Divorce
Centre has done this afternoon, that there is a great principle involved, when the house has already decided to establish no divorce courts in the other provinces? I wonder if my friends realize, first, that this is the only court to which they can go; secondly, that that court consists of two branches of our parliament; thirdly, that one branch of that parliament, through a committee, determines for or against the relief that is asked; and lastly that this house is now merely sending a bill to a committee, which committee may itself determine whether it will utilize the evidence that was given before the senate committee or hear the evidence on its own behalf. And then the bill comes back to the committee of the whole house, which treats it as any other legislation is treated, whether it be legislation relating to patents, to the incorporation of a railway company, or any other question. And that is the reason that the senate committee reduces the evidence to writing, because otherwise there would be no record of it; they might be satisfied with the evidence but there would be nothing in writing upon which to proceed. For that reason they reduce the evidence to writing, submitting it to this house in printed form in order that our committee, following a long established practice extending over twenty-five, thirty, forty and fifty years, may have the evidence before it. It was the same in England. I wonder if my hon. friends realize that before the act of 1857 all divorces considered in Great Britain from any part of the British Isles-from Ireland, from Scotland, from England itself-were by way of private bill which was first heard by a committee of the House of Lords. It was from that practice that we adopted our procedure in this country, of having the evidence heard in a committee of the senate in the first place. That committee of the House of Lords heard the evidence and the appropriate committee in the commons could do what they pleased with it; they could consider the evidence as presented to them, if it were printed, or could themselves hear the witnesses, have the evidence taken down, and arrive at their own conclusion.
I do submit that the observations of the Minister of Railways with respect to the dignity-and shall I say the usefulness-of this parliament were very relevant and most pertinent. Many hon. gentlemen in this house, on conscientious grounds, not believing in divorce and desiring, as they always have desired in days gone by, to maintain their opposition, allow the passage of these bills with the qualification, "carried on division,"
thereby indicating that they do not become a party to the action of this house in granting any divorce; and I am satisfied that these hon. gentlemen have no wish to see the institutions of this country waste time, involving thousands of dollars, in dealing with a question which after all, if it is carefully analyzed, will be seen to be a problem in respect to which we are following not only practice and custom but a rule which, I think it will be admitted, common sense dictates-namely, that where evidence is given under oath before a committee of the senate it is desirable that we dispense, so far as this house is concerned, with the calling of witnesses and the duplicating of evidence received under cross-examination in another branch of parliament.
There is another phase of the question which I desire to put to the house in all seriousness. This is the only court through which relief can be obtained; and as suggested to me this afternoon by my legal friend from Toronto, an English court has no option but to decide. When the witnesses have been heard, the judge upon the bench must decide the case submitted to him; and a committee of this parliament having been convened in due form, and haying before it these cases to deal with, must consider and dispose of them. The paltry excuses which have been put forward against dealing with the matter might be worthy of a debating class in a small academy, but they are uniworthy of the parliament of Canada, and to that extent I agree with what has been said by the Minister of Railways. Indeed, I have been waiting all afternoon and evening for some hon. member representing the government to discuss the subject; for the government must assume responsibility for the conduct of public business in this parliament. I therefore congratulate the minister upon what he has said and upon the stand he has taken, and I trust that hon. gentlemen who have used these methods, from a conscientious desire to hold up to the country the Igck of facilities which they say are afforded people to obtain divorces to which they are entitled, will now realize that, this house having deprived such people of these facilities by its deliberate action in declining to create a court, and there being no other method by which redress may be obtained, it is therefore important that a reasonable course be pursued such as will enable that redress to be given without further delay on the part of, parliament.

I think there is a good deal in what the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) has said as well as

Procedure Respecting Divorce
in the remarks of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett); but I do not know that they have said it all. I had a rather unique honour thrust upon me a few days ago when I was selected, as one of the members of the private bills committee, to be a representative of that committee, with the pleasure of attending the committee in the senate to hear these divorce cases. There used to be but one committee in the senate, and apparently it could handle all cases that came before it. Now business has grown so great over there that the senate has felt it necessary to have three committees on divorce. And we used to have two representatives from the private bills committee whose duty it was to hear such cases; now we have six. I assume the object was to have on each of the three committees in the senate two representatives from the commons committee.
I confess that up to the present time I have not had the time to go to the senate to hear these investigations in respect to this very important matter. In the province of Saskatchewan, from which I have the honour to come, we have a divorce court, and on many occasions my constituents have consulted me with regard to this question, asking me why it was necessary for us to spend our time-or, a3 they put it, waste our time-hearing divorce cases from one or two provinces in Canada. My constituents feel that I am wasting time when I listen to this sort of thing. I agree with the leader of the opposition when he says that there is waste of time; but in my judgment we are wasting time when we proceed in this particular way. This is a matter of great importance and I should like to see every case dealt with fairly and squarely on its merits and a proper decision arrived at. When we dissolve a marriage we dispose of but one phase of the whole question. I have some interest in the women-
Oh, oh.

-whose marriage ties are dissolved. I am sorry that hon. gentlemen opposite laugh. Apparently they have no interest in women; I am different. Let me go one step further and invite them to laugh at this: I have an interest in the children of every marriage which is dissolved. Now I understand that the senate committee has no power, no right, either to deal with alimony for the unfortunate woman or to make a disposition with regard to the children. With all the good intentions in the world, I am bound to say I have not the time seriously to attend the divorce committee in the senate, nor even to report to the private bills com-

mittee of the House of Commons. There is not an hon. member who does not know that this is not possible. Every 'hon. member in this house spends, I believe, from twelve to fifteen hours every day around these buildings during the time this house is in session; and if I attended to the duty which has been thrust upon me and were present at all these meetings of the senate committee on divorce I should be unable to attend to the business for which I was really sent to this house.
Why not resign in favour of the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke)?

Perhaps the
hon. member would like to take the position I now have on the divorce committee. I would resign in favour of the hon. member, and I am sure he would do as badly as I do by force of circumstance. At least I will do this much: whenever I have a little spare time and the senate committee meets for	the consideration	of divorce
cases I will spend that time over there and do what I can. At the same time I am opposed to the method we are adopting; I do not think it is a good practice. But I know of no other way of bringing to the attention of the country the fact that this House of Commons is not doing full justice to the question in failing to place within the grasp of certain provinces-and I agree with the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) that we have not done as we should in this respect-the opportunity of establishing for themselves divorce courts if they so desire. If Ontario and Quebec say that they do not desire divorce courts, at least this house, if this were done, would have gone to the extent of placing them in a position to take advantage of this course as they might see fit. I have given this matter some attention and I think I can stand in this house and say conscientiously and honestly that in the courts of the province of Saskatchewan much more attention is given to these questions than possibly can be given by any committee of this house or of the senate. We are charged by some people with obstructing these bills; some of them get rather warm under the collar because of our actions, but no man can charge any one of us with being less sincere in this matter than he is himself. We are not taking this stand with the idea of obstruction; we are simply drawing to the attention of this country the fact that the present practice is not the proper manner in which marriages should be dissolved, which in my judgment is a very serious business.
While it is not proper for me os a member of this house to review the action taken in connection with another bill or another motion

Procedure Respecting Divorce
which came before the house, perhaps I may be permitted to say that members on all sides should seriously consider, this whole question if ever it comes before the house again. If it seems better to grant divorce courts to those provinces which do not now have them we should seriously consider that situation, and then we would not be confronted with the situation with which we have been faced, this afternoon and this evening. Personally I regret on this or on any other occasion to appear to be delaying the business of this chamber; I have not spent much time talking in this house and I do not propose on any occasion to waste time. However, I do not think we have been wasting time this afternoon or this evening; we are simply using this method of directing the attention of the house to a very undesirable state of affairs in certain provinces of Canada, and I want to place myself on record with regard to the action I have taken.

Mr. Speaker, last year a situation
similar to that with which we have been faced to-day arose in connection with a petition for divorce of which I was the sponsor. That was an attempt on the part of those interested to use obstruction in order to force the hands of the government.

I would remind the hon.
gentleman that the use of the word "obstruction" is not permitted.

I was
merely referring to what happened last year and is happening again this year. Obstruction was resorted to last year in an attempt to force the government to establish such a court as has been suggested, and that is what is being done now. Personally I voted for the establishment of such a court in Ontario, and I would like to see that action taken.

The hon. gentleman is
charging obstruction, and the use of that word is not permitted.
tylr. ANDERSON (High Park): I will withdraw the word; this may be a constructive action on their part, since they want to improve the conditions of affairs, and I think it would be an improvement if this court were established.
The hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) has made himself quite clear; he does not object to these divorce bills being advanced but he would like to see a divorce court established in Ontario. It has been clearly shown to-night and at other times when this subject has been discussed that the
province of Ontario has no court to come to other than the parliament of Canada, and that is a discrimination against the province of Ontario. Some time ago there was a vote on the establishment of divorce courts in Ontario; ninety-nine hon. members voted against such action and sixty-nine voted in favour of it. There was a division among the members who come from Ontario, but another vote took place to-day in which seventy-seven hon. members voted for the advancement of a divorce bill, and there was no division among the Ontario members. So I think the members representing Ontario have shown that this province is desirous of having such a court; that is a reasonable conclusion. But, Mr. Speaker, when I look at the ninety-nine votes cast against the establishment of a divorce court in Ontario I am rather sorry to find that forty-two of those votes were cast by members from the province of Quebec, while not one hon. member from Quebec voted in favour of that measure. I am sure the Quebec members do not wish to be unfair. Ontario has no divorce court and therefore is not on a par with the other provinces of Canada, so it is only fair that Quebec should lend its support to the establishment of these courts. In doing so members from Quebec would not be taking any action which might shake their convictions as to the principle of divorce, because the question of divorce in Quebec is also a local matter. Under our constitution divorce is permissible, and it will remain so until our constitution is amended; such an amendment, which would be a very serious matter, cannot be made except by a bill of this house approved by the various provinces of Canada, since the constitution is founded upon the agreement which was arrived at between the original provinces.
All this would seem to lead to the conclusion that we will continue to have divorce in this country. We have divorce courts in six provinces, and divorce is permissible in the provinces of Ontario, Quebec and Prince Edward Island upon application to this parliament. Some hon. members have stated that they are entirely opposed to the granting of divorces, and the only way to get over that objection is to amend the constitution. It is quite unfair to bring in that argument on these individual applications; the constitution cannot be amended in that way. The constitution is here; it clearly defines our jurisdiction; it is clearly shown and well understood that divorce is heTe and will be granted no matter what we may do in this house. If divorces cannot be secured properly they will

Procedure Respecting Divorce
be granted in some roundabout way. Why should we force the people of the provinces of Ontario, Quebec and Prince Edward Island; to go to the United States or some other place in order to obtain a divorce? I submit that it is very improper for us to force them to take this action by refusing to give Ontario divorce courts and by refusing to grant divorces here at Ottawa.
May I ask a question? Has the legislature of Ontario, the legislature of Quebec or the legislature of Prince Edward Island ever petitioned to obtain these divorce courts?

I am very glad my hon. friend has brought up that point. The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), with whose views I am not always in accord but with whom I agree on this point, stated in his address that the bill providing for the establishing of divorce courts in Ontario should have been amended in order to make it optional with the province of Ontario as to whether or not they should accept those courts. If the province of Ontario has not asked specifically for the establishment of that court, this parliament can create it anyway; we can appoint the judge and it is up to the province to provide the court house and the other officials. The greatest expense is the salary of the judge, which is paid by the Dominion government, and if this jurisdiction is given the supreme court judges there will be no extra expense. Other legislation has been imposed upon the province of Ontario and other provinces without their consent; as examples we have old age pensions and rural credits.
No, no.

Ontario is contributing to the cost of the rural credit scheme and it has not accepted the principle. If a divorce court is good for the whole Dominion why would it not be good for one, two or three provinces? I am satisfied that Ontario will not refuse the court if we create it. The cost to the province will be so small that they can readily fall into line. If the Dominion government is prepared to pay the salary of the justice who will administer the divorce law, I am quite sure the province will provide the court houses and pay the salaries of the minor officers.
The hon. member is discussing a matter which has been determined already by the house.

We have been out of
order all day.

We are discussing one
particular bill of a long list of private bills. The members who discuss this bill are supposed to be familiar with the particulars of it, and they should confine their remarks to the bill. However, as I remarked this afternoon, it is a moot question as to how to distinguish between the general principle of divorce and the particular bill for the granting of a divorce which is now before the house. I would ask hon. gentlemen to confine their remarks as nearly as possible to the present bill.

I accept
Your Honour's ruling although I think there is great justification for my dwelling upon the features of this question. There is no doubt that the action which has been taken with regard to this bill is brought about by the action taken by the house on a former occasion. There is no doubt that the senate committee have arrived at a proper conclusion with regard to this bill. The argument put forth that there is not time to peruse the evidence in connection with these cases is an absolute fallacy, because in most of these cases the evidence is very short. The average case could be read over in about fifteen minutes; for I do not think it takes over twenty-five minutes for the senate committee to hear every word uttered by the members of that committee, the counsel and the witnesses connected with the average case. Copies of evidence are sent to every member of the house, and they can. read them if they so desire. I had not seen this particular application until this evening, but I got it from my file and read it in a few minutes while sitting here in the house. There is no doubt that this divorce should be granted. These people are put to very great expense, many of them coming from outside of the country; they are taking the law as they find it and as it is administered, and why should we take the position of preventing them from obtaining their divorces?
I am in sympathy with those who are opposing this bill, because I believe their motive is the establishment of a divorce court in Ontario. At the same time, I think the same result could be obtained by proceeding along a different line, and I believe if the amendment suggested by the hon. member for La-belle (Mr. Bourassa) were accepted it would overcome all our difficulties. I do not desire to say that the hon. member has been using obstructive methods, because that is unparliamentary language, and I believe he desires to bring about a result which would be beneficial to the people. I might refer to an-

Procedure Respecting Divorce
other matter which was obstructed last year, and the principle was accepted this year and went through the house without any objection.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has convinced me that I should uphold this corner of the house in opposing the passing of these divorce bills. He said that there was no other court to which these people could apply, but that court is only half a court.

The court I mentioned
was the high court of parliament consisting of both houses.
It is only half a court because it cannot grant what a proper divorce court could grant. This court of parliament can only grant divorces; it cannot grant alimony or give justice and equity.
I would point out to the hon. member that such relief has been asked for, only in one instance, and parliament dealt with that case.
It is not asked for because it is not within the power of this parliament to grant it, owing to the fact it interferes with provincial matters. That question has never come up.
It has come up.

Only in one instance, and that was occasioned by an oversight. The hon. member said that there was no other court to which they could apply, and because this court is only half a court and cannot give equity and justice, there is one of two things which we should do. We should grant the divorce court of parliament power to enable them to allow alimony and deal with these people on a basis of justice and equity. If we cannot do that, we should send these people to a court where they can get full justice. As things exist at the present time, when they go through this court they are forced to apply to the civil courts in Ontario to obtain alimony. As the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) said, this is the only method we can employ to draw the attention of the public and of this parliament to the necessity of doing one of the two things I mentioned.
As the hon. member who has just taken his seat has said, it is quite true that it would take only about fifteen minutes for a member to read this evidence. There are about 300 cases, and 300 times fifteen minutes equals seventy-five hours. I for one am not going to spend seventy-five hours in reading this evidence. I went up to my room to-night with
the idea of obtaining some information with regard to these bills, and I spent five or ten minutes tiying to find the particular bill. As the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) has said, my constituents do not send me to parliament to spend seventy-five hours of my time in reading divorce evidence. I do not like obstructive tactics, but I see no other way by which the attention of the house and of the country can be drawn to the fact that we should either reform our present methods or provide a separate court to pass upon these applications for divorce.

Mr. Speaker,
I sometimes find great difficulty in understanding how men reach certain conclusions, and the speech which has been delivered by the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Adshead) is an excellent illustration of that difficulty. When the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) spoke, following as he did the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning),
I felt that he had made such a conclusive and absolutely clear statement that the opposition from the corner of the house would have seen the light. But it would seem that while the speeches made by the two hon. members I have mentioned made one impression upon my mind, they made an entirely different impression upon the mind of the hon. member for East Calgary. The house is to be congratulated that the leader of the opposition and the Minister of Railways stated the matter as clearly as they did. I felt very keenly this afternoon that the actions of the house were not in harmony with the best traditions of parliament, or consonant with the dignity of the house.

Was the hon. member
in the house when the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) was speaking?

I was. Since the hon.
member for Battle River has asked how I regard the speech of the hon. member for Saskatoon, I may say that I agree with him up to a certain point, just as I said, when I spoke first this afternoon, that I agreed with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) up to a certain point. We may candidly admit that they did a service in bringing to the attention of the house the absolutely absurd situation that exists in parliament with regard to the question of divorce, but I cannot follow them to the extreme to which they have gone. They having made their protest, I think, we should proceed to deal with the business of the house in somewhat the same manner as we have

Procedure Respecting Divorce
been accustomed to dealing with it in the past and not change the rules of the game after the game has started.
There was one point I wanted to mention this afternoon but to which I omitted any reference, that is, the obligation of this house toward the people who have brought these bills before parliament. That is something we should consider very seriously. These are private bills. Any private individual in Canada has a right to come to parliament and ask for any legislation he sees fit. It rests with parliament to decide the merits of the case and to determine whether or not the legislation sought shall be granted. A large number of people, how many I do not yet know, have come to parliament in all good faith, and they have a right to assume that parliament will deal with these matters in somewhat the same way as we have dealt with them in the past. The question of establishing a divorce court in Ontario has been injected into this debate. Unfortunately hon. members in that corner of the house, the hon. member for Saskatoon and one or two more, assume that that question is an issue before the house. It is not, and it cannot be made an issue before the house at this session if I understand parliamentary procedure aright, because the house has already decided it. It may be made an issue next session, and from the discussion that has taken place this afternoon I am quite sure that the question will be before the house next session when I fully anticipate that a different decision will be reached. But I should like to remind those hon. members that it is not and cannot be made an issue before us at the present time. We can take whatever position we please on these particular bills, but if I am correct in my interpretation, we cannot establish that court this session. Perhaps better parliamentary authorities than I am will confirm or question my statement as they see fit. That, however, is my understanding of the situation. We have to deal with the facts as we find them and the fact is that a large number of people in all good faith have come before parliament and sought relief, as it is called, from the particular disabilities under which they labour. Hon. members assume that they have a right to vote against these bills because they have not the evidence before them. I take the other ground. As I stated this afternoon, evidence has been given before a committee of another house, and I take the position that unless it can be clearly shown, or unless there is some reason to believe, that a proper decision has not been rendered, we have a right to accept the judgment of that committee.
[Mr. Brown 1
On two or three occasions since I have been in the house and also a member of the private bills committee, there have come before that committee cases where there was some disagreement with the judgment rendered by the senate committee. Those questions were dealt with on their merits. It might be that the judgment of the senate committee was upheld, or the reverse. That is the course open to us now. Let us remember that this is a private bill. The principle was laid down two years ago, when we discussed the ''leorgian bay canal bill, that the second reading of a private bill was always granted unless there was opposition to the principle of the bill. That is a statement which is in harmony with the best parliamentary authorities. Hon. members opposing these particular bills are not opposed to the principle of the bill, that is, the principle of divorce. It is true that some members are. My controversy at the moment is not with, them, but rather with those who are following the leadership of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The principle of the bill is not questioned by them. Therefore, in the very nature of the case these bills should receive their second reading and should go to the private bills committee where, if there is any particular bill to which any hon. member objects or if he thinks in regard to any particular bill the senate committee has not rendered the best judgment according to the evidence, he can bring the matter up and have it dealt with. Otherwise I think we are warranted in accepting the position that the senate committee in making its recommendation has dealt fairly, justly, and according to the evidence.
I want to fall back again upon my other statement. A number of people have come before parliament in good faith, feeling they have a right to expect we will deal with them in much the same way as we have dealt with others in the past. It is quite evident that the course that is proposed by certain hon. members is to institute a blockade by which these people will be deprived of their rights or of the relief which they have a right to expect.
Mr. WOOD9WORTH: I rise to a point of order. The hon. member for Lisgar has suggested certain motives on our part, namely, that we are trying to create a blockade in order to prevent the passage of these bills.
I object decidedly to that. That is not my purpose, and I do not think it is right that an hon. member should impute motives of that kind to another hon. member. I ask that the expression be withdrawn.

Procedure Respecting Divorce

I am not charging the hon. member with instituting a blockade, but I am stating what the inevitable result of this particular course of conduct will be, if they insist on calling a vote and discussing every one of these bills as he has indicated he intends doing.

The expressions "blockade" and "obstruction" are not parliamentary, and whatever may be the result of opposition, as long as the opposition is legitimate it cannot be qualified as a blockade or obstruction.
I certainly do not wish to use any terms that are unparliamentary, but I am pointing out that that is the inevitable result of the course outlined by these hon members.
Withdraw.

I have withdrawn to the best of mv ability. I say that I do not wish to use an unparliamentary term, and if the term "deliberate blockade" is unparliamentary,
I withdraw it.

They are
very sensitive when we tell them the truth.
Yes, they do not like the truth.
I rise to a point of order.
I should like the hon. member not to charge other hon. members as not liking the truth. If they do not like the truth, what, do they like?
I withdraw that. They do not always like to have the clear consequences of their conduct pointed out to them.
They prefer darkness to light.

The inevitable result of the course outlined by themselves will be that many of these bills cannot be passed through this house, because it is physically impossible for us to deal with so many in such a manner. We cannot take a vote on every one of them on the second reading, then have them go to the private bills committee and be discussed there and come back to the house for their third reading. As I say, the inevitable result will be that they cannot be passed through the house, and consequently the people who have come here in good faith, incurred the expense involved in the house and in connection with lawyers' fees, which in most cases are by no means small, will be treated in a manner that is grossly unfair. Unless there is reason to believe that the
evidence taken before the senate committee is faulty, I think we are quite justified in accepting it and granting these people relief.
These are the reasons why I shall give my support to the passage of these divorce bills through the house. While I would strongly support, and did when the other bill was before the house, the establishment of a divorce court to deal with these cases-undoubtedly a court could deal with them better, could go into the question of alimony, for instance -we cannot get these courts at this time, and therefore I say let us, in a manner becoming to the dignity of this honourable house, deal with the situation that confronts us.

Is the argument of the
hon. member that if we consider these bills properly they will not get through this session, and therefore we should put them through without proper consideration?

That is not my argument.
From the very beginning I have said that these cases are dealt with properly before the senate committee, where the evidence is taken, and if any hon. member feels that in any particular case the judgment of the senate committee is not in harmony with the evidence, he can bring that case before the private bills committee, and it will be dealt with there.
Have I to spend seventyfive hours going into the details of all these cases?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) does me rather an unmerited honour when he suggests-

Has the hon. member
not already spoken on this bill?

No, your honour.
I think I have a right to speak on this bill.
Yes.

And on all
the others.
And on all the others.

And he
probably will.

As I was saying,
the hon. member for Lisgar has done me a somewhat unmerited honour in suggesting that the members of the house who have spoken against this method of granting divorces are following the leadership of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I am only an individual member, but I venture

Procedure Respecting Divorce
to suggest that others who have spoken along the same lines, have done so simply because the merits of the case appeal to them-for that and for no other reason.
The hon. member for Lisgar suggests that bills should be dealt with this year in the same way that they have been dealt with in previous years. I am at a loss to know why he should make a statement of that kind. I can think of the Sun Life bill and the Bell Telephone bill which during the past two or three years were dealt with in a very, very different way from that in which bills of that kind were dealt with for a great many years in this house. I can think of railway bills which during the last two or three years have been dealt with in a very different way from the way in which they were dealt with for many years in this house when we were so lavish in granting railway charters. So there have been changes, and I think we are quite within our rights in insisting that these divorce bills should receive fair attention.
These bills were not before the house last year.

That is why, since the matter has been referred to, I may be permitted to employ two or three minutes of my time in regard to it.
When the question of a divorce court for Ontario came up, I made it quite clear that I was opposed on principle to divorce; that I was opposed to the establishment of divorce courts everywhere. But since divorce courts have been established in seven out of the nine provinces of Canada in esse or in posse,- because in Prince Edward Island they voted long before confederation for the establishment of a divorce court and they have it in posse if not in esse-I stated and I repeat to-night, and the sense of the house and the sense of the country will have to come to it: the only real remedy for this situation, which has grown upon us and which will be far worse next year, and the year after, than it is this year, is to come back to the true moral and social basis of confederation: wipe off from clause 91 the subsection enabling or, rather, forcing-because in that respect I agree with the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan)-forcing this parliament to deal with divorce. Let us go back to the principle, the spirit of confederation, and let us wipe off those three words: "Marriage and divorce' from clause 91.
It has been said by the hon. member for Toronto High Park (Mr. Anderson):	"But
you cannot do it unless the provinces agree to it." Why? We can not take away any of the rights of the provinces without their consent, but we can always renounce some of our own rights; and. after that, the provinces can, under another disposition of the British North America Act, amend their own constitution according to their needs. Once this parliament, by a joint address of both houses, decides that it will have no more to do with
f.Mr. Bourassa.]
divorce, either in a legislative capacity or in its capacity of creating courts of justice to adjudicate upon divorce, then the provinces are free, each of them according to its views, according to what it considers to be in the best interest of the local community for which its government is responsible, to decide whether or not they will maintain the divorce courts they have or, if they do not have them, create them. This is a practical remedy. I mentioned it during the first debate. I mention it again to-night, not with the hope, of course, that it will be voted upon right away. Perhaps some hon. members who would be disposed to agree to it would not like to receive it from such unholy hands as those of the man who is speaking now. But the time will surely come, and let it come as soon as possible, when individuals and groups and parties being forgotten, some sensible individual, no eccentric or crank of my nature, but some sensible individual accepted as a wise man by everybody, will stand up and propose this remedy; and then it will be jumped at by all the wiseacres of the land; because, I repeat, this is the only manner in which you can at once simplify the operations of this house and return the two branches of this parliament to their proper functions, and at the same time strike off from the constitution that anomaly which leaves a portion of our matrimonial law in the hands of the provinces while keeping another portion here. It was a nonsensical disposition adopted in the last hours of the discussion on the confederation bill. As a matter of fact, it was not in the resolutions of Quebec; it was not in the de-cisisons taken by the parliament of United Canada. It was grafted upon the constitution, like that absurd clause 93 with regard to sdhools, in London, in order to conciliate the views of this church and that church, of this group and 'that; and like all that kind of patchwork it could not work. So long as the population was limited the number of people seeking divorce was not numerous, therefore we did not feel the absurdity or the pinch of the system; but now it is upon us.
I cannot agree with my good friend from Lisgar, who proposes that we let the present system go on for this year. No, sir. If we do not bring it home to every member of this house and to the people whom we represent, the same thing will go on year after year. It will never be remedied until parliament realizes that we are in an impossible situation and thait we must treat it in a radical manner from a double point of view-one of principle and one of practice equally.
